security_audit.summary: Static findings were a mix of normal serial-device tooling and high-risk dual-use exploitation guidance. I confirmed the critical workflows around password file access, SSH persistence, backdoor accounts, bootloader root-shell bypass, credential searches, firmware extraction, network reconnaissance, and shell=True trigger execution; I dismissed documentation links, Markdown backticks, normal /dev/ttyUSB use, and log cleanup as false positives. Static review was capped at 400/457 representative findings; omitted static matches are unconfirmed, so automatic publishing stays disabled until manual review.

remediation.suggestion: Manually review the omitted 57 static analyzer matches or reduce bundled generated/vendor/reference content before enabling automatic publication.

remediation.issue: Persistence and backdoor instructions are included in user-facing examples.
remediation.suggestion: Remove instructions for adding root SSH keys, UID 0 users, reverse shells, and startup backdoors.

remediation.issue: Bootloader examples show authentication bypass into a root shell.
remediation.suggestion: Replace root-shell bypass steps with safe bootloader hardening checks and authorization reminders.

remediation.issue: Credential and key discovery commands search sensitive files across the target filesystem.
remediation.suggestion: Limit examples to detecting exposed secrets in controlled fixtures or redact commands that harvest real credentials.

remediation.issue: Firmware dumping examples include transfer to another host.
remediation.suggestion: Frame firmware capture as explicit owner-approved backup only and remove netcat exfiltration examples.

remediation.issue: The helper runs trigger scripts through subprocess.run with shell=True.
remediation.suggestion: Parse trigger commands into argv lists or require an explicit allowlist before executing external triggers.

remediation.issue: Default examples store session logs under shared temporary paths.
remediation.suggestion: Use private log directories with restrictive permissions when logs may contain credentials or device identifiers.

content.user_title: Audit IoT UART Consoles with picocom
content.value_statement: UART testing can be slow when serial output is noisy and difficult to capture. This skill guides authorized serial sessions with logging, prompt detection, and structured embedded device checks.
actual_capabilities: Connects to UART consoles through picocom or the included Python serial helper.
Runs single commands, interactive sessions, batch command files, and passive monitor captures.
Detects prompts, cleans terminal output, and can produce structured command results.
Logs serial input and output for review during authorized embedded device testing.
Documents workflows for boot logs, AT command interfaces, BusyBox shells, and U-Boot consoles.
Provides observation guidance for watching serial sessions from another terminal.
limitations: Requires physical serial access, the correct adapter wiring, and permission to test the device.
Depends on local tools such as picocom, Python, pyserial, screen, or socat.
Some examples are high risk and require strict authorization before use.
Session logs can contain secrets and must be stored with restrictive permissions.

use_cases.title: Capture Boot Logs
use_cases.description: Record boot output from an embedded device and identify prompts, baud issues, and startup services.

use_cases.title: Inspect Authorized Consoles
use_cases.description: Run controlled commands on a lab device and preserve a session transcript for a security report.

use_cases.title: Test Modem AT Interfaces
use_cases.description: Send AT commands to cellular or satellite modems and classify normal, error, and connection responses.

prompt_templates.title: Start a Basic UART Session
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for an authorized device.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the picocom skill to connect to my authorized device on /dev/ttyUSB0 at 115200 baud. Capture the first prompt and summarize what you see.

prompt_templates.title: Monitor Boot Output
prompt_templates.scenario: Passive capture while a device starts.
prompt_templates.prompt: Monitor the UART output for 60 seconds while I reboot the device. Save a session log and summarize boot stages, prompts, and errors.

prompt_templates.title: Run a Controlled Enumeration

best_practices: Use this skill only on devices you own or have written authorization to test.
Store session logs outside shared temporary paths when they may contain secrets.
Start with passive monitoring before running commands that change device state.
anti_patterns: Do not use persistence, backdoor, or shell escape examples on systems without explicit authorization.
Do not publish raw session logs because they may include passwords, keys, or device identifiers.
Do not assume one baud rate, prompt pattern, or line ending works for every embedded device.

faq.question: What does this skill help me do?
faq.answer: It helps run and observe authorized UART serial sessions for embedded and IoT security testing.

faq.question: Does it require hardware access?
faq.answer: Yes. You need a serial adapter, correct wiring, and permission to connect to the device.

faq.question: Can it use Claude, Codex, and Claude Code?
faq.answer: Yes. The report declares support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code compatible workflows.

faq.question: Can it monitor without sending commands?
faq.answer: Yes. Monitor mode can passively capture UART output for a chosen duration.

faq.question: Why are logs a security concern?
faq.answer: Serial logs can contain passwords, tokens, keys, network details, and device identifiers.

faq.question: Is this safe for any device?
faq.answer: No. Some workflows can change device state and must be limited to approved lab testing.
